source.title: Training Large Language Models for Small-Molecule Design with Synthetic Task Scaling
source.authors: Frank Hu; Shriram Chennakesavalu; Zi-Cheng Wang; Patricia Suriana; Bodhi P. Vani; Kirill Shmilovich; Kang-Way V. Chuang; Colin A. Grambow

record.tranche_reason: The study discusses synthetic task scaling and cites pretraining scaling work, but it does not test held-out cross-entropy scaling or any listed claim version. Its own relevant results compare molecular-design task performance across post-training recipes and training wall time.
record.gate_note: The paper cites Kaplan et al. and discusses scaling synthetic post-training tasks. Its own cost-versus-performance results concern relative binding-affinity improvement on molecular design tasks, not held-out language-model loss, model size, or a compute-optimal parameter/token allocation. Those related results are recorded with versions ["none"].
record.test_reason: The paper post-trains a 35B-A3B MoE model with RLVR on synthetic molecular-design tasks and compares recipes by binding-affinity improvement and wall time. It does not measure held-out pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute, so it does not test any version. It only cites Kaplan et al. as background.
record.authors_conclusion: Correct. The authors say curriculum training on cheap synthetic tasks, then harder ones, improves SQM lead optimization and beats larger frontier models. They also say they see no clear scaling law between training cost (wall time) and performance.
record.recipe_differences: Uses post-training RLVR on synthetic chemistry tasks and curriculum mixtures, rather than a language-model pretraining sweep of parameter count, tokens, compute, or held-out cross-entropy.
record.method_sensitivity: Molecular-design outcomes vary with curriculum recipe and reward weighting; the authors report that alternative reward weightings perform worse on the SQM evaluation.

fits_no_version.finding: Across post-training recipes (500 steps each, same 35B-A3B model), the authors see no clear scaling law between training wall time (about 70-80 h) and molecular-design binding-affinity improvement (Figure 3 right, Table 2). The performance metric is not pretraining loss.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: For this fixed-size model and molecular-design setup, longer post-training wall time does not produce a clear monotonic performance trend.

record.problems: The experiments start from one model family and size and do not sweep pretraining parameters, tokens, compute, or held-out cross-entropy. The paper reports standard errors for the molecular-design metric, but those measurements do not establish the listed language-model scaling claims.

untested.parts: No pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No fit on small runs, no prediction of larger runs.
No fixed-compute split of parameters and tokens.
No architecture shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
RL post-training is used, but no power-law form is fitted for loss or any other metric.
Downstream performance is measured only for one model size, not versus scale or pretraining loss.
No exponents or compute-optimal split are fitted or compared.

record.verdict_notes: The paper is outside the scope of the scaling_laws claim. The wall-time remark concerns post-training recipes with a fixed step count, not scale in parameters, tokens or loss, so it is not evidence on V5 or V7. The rows R1-R11 are correctly linked to none.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out pretraining loss sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No prediction of larger-run loss from fits on smaller runs.
No architecture-shape comparison at fixed parameter count.
The study uses post-training RL, but does not test whether loss follows the same power-law form in that regime.
It evaluates downstream molecular-design performance, but does not test its predictability from model scale or pretraining loss.
No power-law exponents or compute-optimal split are fit or compared.
